newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Buba frees repo business from reserve requirement.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Buba frees repo business from reserve requirement.

text.p: The German central bank on Thursday relaxed its reserve policies in order to improve the German market's international competitiveness, pleasing market participants who had long lobbied for the step.

"I am absolutely delighted. The most important aspect of this move is that such a measure boosts the financial centre of Frankfurt without harming monetary policy," said Hermann Remsperger, chief economist at BHF Bank in Frankfurt.
From January 1, the Bundesbank will no longer demand that banks hold reserves in non-interest bearing accounts at the central bank on a portion of their business, a rule in force since 1948.

"The exemption of repo business with maturities of up to one year from the minimum reserve will strengthen the efficiency and competitiveness of the German market," the Bundesbank said in a statement.

The central bank however said the move would only lead to a small cut in the overall minimum reserve requirements as banks will still need to hold a portion of short-term sight and savings deposits at the central bank.

Reserves are designed to help the Bundesbank better steer monetary policy and until now banks have had to hold reserves of two percent on repo business and sight deposits and 1.5 percent on savings deposits.

Thursday's relaxation also does not mean Germany has abandoned its concept of holding minimum reserves altogether the Bundesbank said, insisting it will continue to press the future European Central Bank to use the instruments.
The Bundesbank is currently the only central bank in an industrialised European nations that requires banks to hold reserves in non-interest bearing accounts.

Under a repo transaction, a dealer borrows funds from an investor by selling securities to him. The dealer repurchases the securities at a later date, thereby repaying the loan. The difference between the sale and repurchase price represents interest on the loan.
While bankers were generally delighted with the move, they admitted the decision may be more of a boost for Germany's image than breathe life back into a largely dormant repo market.

Peter Coym, management board member at Lehman Brothers Bankhaus in Frankfurt and board member of the Association of Foreign Banks said: "It's a positive move and will definitely help Germany as a financial centre, but I'm sceptical that it will lead to a return of repo business on a major scale."
Nonetheless, bankers hope the new rule will help bring back some of the repo business they have lost to centres like London.

Commerzbank economist Juergen Pfister told Reuters Financial Television: "A lot of this business already takes place outside Germany. But over the next 12 to 18 months, business will start to move back to Germany."
Bankers however agreed the step could make their lives easier if their banks decide to consolidate trading desks.
Many German banks have repo trading desks in London as well as Frankfurt and such double desking may now become unnecessary, one trader said.
